records.text: pan, BNP Paribas Fig. 3: BoJ balance sheet (JPY trn) JGB reduction implies significant decline in reserves Of the JPY2.1tron monthly purchase amount, JPY100bn is for JGBs with maturities under one year and therefore exits the balance sheet within a year. The remaining JPY2trn stays on the balance sheet for a longer period. Consequently, the BoJ’s JGB holdings would increase by JPY2trn × 12 = JPY24trn per year. The average remaining maturity of the BoJ’s JGB portfolio is currently 6.4 years, so a simple calculation gives 6.4 years x JPY24trn/year = JPY153.6trn. This figure could be viewed as the steady-state level of BoJ JGB holdings if the JPY2.1trn monthly purchase volume were maintained after Q1-2027. Reducing the JGB holdings to this extent would also considerably compress the BoJ’s balance sheet. As of the end of March-2026, the BoJ’s balance sheet comprises: JGBs: JPY530.9trn Various operations (pooled-collateral, loan-support, etc.): JPY77.7 trn ETFs: JPY37.1trn The ETF holdings are slated for a gradual draw-down; the pace is very slow, so the impact on the balance sheet over the next few years will be minimal. Loan-support programs are also being phased out for new tranches, so their balances are expected to fall gradually. We see three reasons why the 10-week closure of the Strait of Hormuz has hurt global growth only moderately so far. First, oil prices have not risen as much as expected, partly because of unusually high pre-war inventories and partly because markets never lost faith that very large consumer price hikes would prompt a US policy shift. Second, physical shortages in areas such as jet fuel have so far been met with relatively painless forms of demand destruction (e.g. a large shift to renewables in China and reduced flight schedules on lower-value routes globally). Third, fiscal policy, the AI boom, and—with a brief interruption in March—financial conditions have been supportive all year. Under our baseline assumption of a gradual Strait reopening that starts soon and finishes in late June, we see Brent prices stable in the near term and edging down to $90/barrel by year-end. However, the risks remain tilted toward more adverse outcomes, higher oil prices, and greater economic damage. 2. records.text: What is at stake? In March 2024, the European Central Bank revised its operational framework, preparing the ground for a transition from abundant excess liquidity to a less ample regime. We explored the design features and market implications of this shift in ECB Operational Framework: Sticking to the floor, dated 7 March 2024. With the 2026 review of key framework parameters in sight, this note takes stock of how the ECB approach compares internationally, how the next stage of balance sheet normalisation may unfold – and what estimates suggest about a plausible range for ‘optimal’ liquidity under the new regime. A framework to avoid a number: The ECB has been explicit: it does not want to anchor policy implementation to a predefined stock of excess reserves. In a post- QE environment, reserve demand is shaped by regulation, payment behaviour and precautionary motives, making it unstable and difficult to estimate ex ante. Instead, the ECB has designed a framework through which the level of reserves is revealed endogenously by banks’ recourse to refinancing operations. Where quantification has been attempted, staff scenarios suggest a very wide range of excess reserve demand – roughly EUR600bn–EUR2.2trn – underscoring that ‘optimal’ is not a point estimate but a function of banks’ liquidity preferences. records.text: The AI investment boom’s Asia spillovers The AI capex boom has benefited chip and server producers across Asia. We quantified the very large boost to Taiwan (and to a lesser extent South Korea and Vietnam) in previous analysis. However, we are sometimes asked about the likely future impact, and other potential beneficiaries in the region. In this piece, we trace the impact on the broader Asia tech ecosystem, and also try to project forward the likely boost to growth given AI capex expectations.1 Taiwan is the regional (and global) standout but other notable beneficiaries include South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, and Vietnam. Spending on AI-related investment has surged in recent years, with the release of ChatGPT in late 2022 a notable catalyst. Following Q1 earnings reports, consensus estimates now expect the five largest ‘hyperscalers’ in the US to invest $750bn in 2026, predominantly in data centers (Exhibit 1). Global AI-related capex is of course significantly larger than this, both because these five companies do not represent all US AI capex, and because there are significant investments occurring in other parts of the world. For 2026, AI capex will likely be well over $1tn globally. However, the ‘hybrid’ methodology (first introduced in 2019, changed in 2024) made Euribor a lot more volatile, even in ample liquidity conditions since it is transactions based and transactions are scarce. In the absence of transactions, submissions rely on the former day(s) data, which, under volatile market conditions may cause erratic movements in the fixing. By construction, the fixing may thus take time to reflect changed liquidity and credit conditions, even more so since the ‘expert judgement’ has been removed from its methodology. MMF assets are another important source of liquidity to keep in consideration as well as a barometer of credit conditions. A growing economy and little uncertainty would typically favour tight bases, in opposition with rising default rates and difficult access to funding. 2 Liquid Insight | 11 May 2026 Thinking the unthinkable: US hike risk We offer frameworks to think about conditions for Fed hikes, how many hikes the market can price near-term, & broader US rate implications of this shifting risk. Conditions for Fed hikes: Frameworks = (1) BofA economists (2) Fed SEP. BofA economists view: “For hikes to be on the table under Warsh, we think the u-rate would need to fall to/below 4% and core PCE would need to get closer to 3.5%, even as tariff effects roll off the y/y rate. The case for hikes would strengthen if wages start accelerating again, or inflation expectations de-anchor” (see report: Change in Fed call). Fed summary of economic projections (SEP): the SEP at end '26 showed no participant expecting a hike, the lowest unemployment rate forecast of 4.3%, & highest core PCE f'cst of 3.0%. We can infer it would take U3 <=4.2% & core PCE >=3.0% to justify hikes. Both variables are likely trending in that direction. Hike pricing: Frameworks = (1) recent history (2) Fed cuts in ’25 (3) Taylor rule. Recent history: Market pricing for '26 hikes previously reached 3.78% (14bps of hikes) with less certainty on macro data. 14bps in '26 could easily repeat. Fed cuts in ’25: the Fed cut 75bps in late '25 due to concerns about a softening labor market. Indeed, Fed cuts were triggered by 6m NFP average falling <30k. Today 6m NFP average is running 55k and trending upwards (Exhibit 2). Fed risk balance is shifting to upside inflation > downside labor.

records.text: Other approaches A third general approach, fairly closely related to the second, is to calculate net real tech exports. It’s important to recognize that tech imports can be used either as inputs into production of exports, or for domestic investment or consumption. We need to subtract the latter portions so we can compare the net value creation in exports (i.e. we want real tech exports – real tech imports used in those exports). This again involves using OECD data to estimate the import (and tech import) share of domestic demand. It further requires “double deflation” – deflation of exports and imports using price indices for each. We found these estimates to be similar to method 2 in most cases, but with more variation across countries, so we do not present them here. Finally, additional approaches are sometimes possible where unique data sets exist. For example, Taiwan and Korea directly report nominal and real tech value-added.9 This can be used to estimate tech sector contributions up to that period, in a manner similar to method 1, and then extrapolated based on tech output or exports. For Korea, we used a proxy for chip performance (‘bit shipments’) to estimate/forecast a real production series for AI-related tech goods—this also resulted in a 2025 estimate reassuringly similar to our other approaches. It explicitly avoids anchoring to a numerical threshold, viewing reserve demand as uncertain and structurally evolving. Scarcity is expected to be identified ex post, through price and quantity signals – rather than prevented ex ante by maintaining a large balance sheet. Bottom line: Both systems aim to operate with ample reserves, but whereas the Fed manages scarcity risk primarily through balance-sheet size, the ECB does so through operational elasticity. The former stays safely above an estimated threshold; the latter relies on controlled access to central bank liquidity when that threshold is approached. As a result, the ECB accepts a greater role for market adjustment as reserves decline, unlike the Fed which aims to minimise scarcity- driven rate volatility through reserve calibration. ECB vs BoE – converging frameworks, different starting points: Both the ECB and the Bank of England are converging towards a demand-driven, repo-led operational framework, but from different points in the transition. At the same time, a potential challenger Angela Rayner has previously suggested £3-4bn of tax rises (including raising the bank surcharge to 5% from 2%, removing inheritance tax relief for AIM shares and reinstating pensions lifetime allowance). If a leadership challenge were to occur, potentially higher spending could support growth but policy uncertainty and possibility of higher taxes or higher borrowing costs could offset some of it. It is worth noting that fiscal pressures are high, no matter who the Labour leader is. Even if there is no change in Labour leadership, there is likely to be fiscal pressure to provide support in response to the energy shock along with public services and defence spending pressures, which may increase further given Labour losses. Risks of non- manifesto tax rises remain in coming years. Moreover, the move higher in yields along with potentially weaker growth or higher inflation is likely to have already hurt the headroom. Having said that, we don't expect the fiscal response to the energy shock to be as forceful as in 2022, given the limited fiscal space. Targeted temporary support to low-income households costing low single-digit billions looks more likely to us.

With the 2026 review of key framework parameters in sight this note takes stock of how ECB approach compares internationally, how the next stages of balances sheet normalizations mya unfold and what scenario-based estimates suggest about a plausible range for ‘optimal’ liquidity under the new regime. A framework to avoid a number. The ECB has been explicit: it does not aim to anchor policy implementation to a predefined stock of excess reserves. In a post post-QE environment, reserve demand is shaped by regulation, payment behaviour and precautionary motives, making it unstable and difficult to estimate ex ante. Rather than calibrating a target quantity, the ECB has designed a framework in which the level of reserves is revealed endogenously through banks’ recourse to refinancing operations. Where quantification has been attempted, staff scenarios suggest a very wide range of excess reserve demand – roughly EUR 600bn to EUR2.2tn – underscoring that ‘optimal’ is not a point estimate but a function of banks’ liquidity preferences. The current 15bp corridor between the MRO and the DFR acts as a guardrail, ensuring rate control while allowing quantities to adjust. In short: the ECB seeks to discover the equilibrium level of reserves, not choose it. Sequencing normalization: behaviour over threshold. Catalyst.Metric: Balance sheet reduction and reserve levels

records.text: the balance sheet is likely to slow to roughly JPY30-40trn per year. Based on these rough outlooks, we can infer that the balance sheet will reach roughly JPY450trn around 2030-2031, and at that point the decline in reserve could trigger an “X-day”—a date on which short-term interest-rate markets are significantly affected. Of course, if purchases are reduced more aggressively, X-day would arrive earlier. If BoJ were to reduce liabilities outside banknotes and reserves (e.g. foreign central bank deposits, government reverse repo) , the X-day will arrive later. Finally, we would like to note the emerging uncertainty around the demand for reserves in a world with positive rates. When negative rates were introduced, Japanese banks seemed to adopt the practice of keeping only the minimal amount of reserves and avoiding holding the negative-rate portion. Recently, however, loan growth has outpaced deposit growth, narrowing the loan-deposit gap (figure 4). Over time, loan growth will fill this gap, reducing banks’ incentives to hold long-dated bonds and increasing incentives to hold shorter-dated JGBs or reserves. Currently, the BoJ holds a plentiful JPY469trn in reserves. records.text: Solving for Diesel Shortages We assess scarcity risks for diesel in the OECD, market pricing, and what could prevent shortages in extended Hormuz closure risk scenarios. The Vulnerable Backbone We see diesel as more vulnerable to the Hormuz shock than gasoline for supply and demand reasons. On the supply side, the sharp drop in exports from the Persian Gulf corresponds to medium and heavy crude oil, which tends to yield more heavy products such as diesel, fuel oil, and jet fuel than lighter Western WTI or Brent crude (Exhibit 1, left). The 8mb/d drop in medium and heavy global crude exports year-to-date more than fully explains the drop in global crude exports (Exhibit 1, right). On the demand side, prices would likely have to rise substantially more for diesel than for gasoline and especially jet fuel and petrochemical feedstocks to generate a given percent reduction in demand (and the more price-sensitive demand for petrochemical feedstocks and jet fuel has already weakened substantially). The price elasticity of demand is likely lower for diesel—sometimes characterized as the “backbone” fuel of the global economy—because it tends to meet essential demand with limited substitutes (Exhibit 2, left). Global demand for diesel—which is mostly used for trucking but also in mining, construction, industry, and agriculture—has historically only dropped sharply in recessions (Exhibit 2, right). We estimate that OECD commercial stocks will decline by around 180 million barrels over that period. The heavier lifting instead comes from strategic inventory releases, which will draw by around 316 million barrels. This distinction matters enormously for price formation. Even if the Strait reopens in June, the seasonal lift in summer demand, combined with the exceptionally large commercial stock draws seen in March and April, and likely again in May, should push OECD inventories toward operational stress levels by August. This is what keeps crude prices elevated in the low $100s through most of the year, rather than allowing a sharp retracement once Hormuz reopens. At the same time, the model offers an important clue as to why crude prices themselves are not materially higher. The implicit message from the framework is that a disruption of this scale cannot be rebalanced solely through the crude market. There simply is not enough elasticity on the crude side alone. Instead, the adjustment increasingly shifts downstream—out of crude and into refined products (Down the barrel, 8 May 2026). The shift is already visible in prices. From January through April, crude prices have risen roughly 40%, while refined product prices in Asia—the region hit hardest so far—have increased by 60% to 120% (Figure 2). records.text: Repo spreads to ESTR – Liquidity matters, so does bond supply: While 9% also seems to coincide with a threshold above which reserves are abundant enough to keep a lid (DFR) on German repo rates, fluctuations are more volatile and dispersed than in the unsecured funding space. The bond collateral leg of the trade indeed plays a crucial role, as we constantly highlight in our research. Our bond supply and QT outlook would suggest further cheapening pressure is on the cards, with potential for German repo to average ESTR +6–8bp in H2 (versus 5bp in H1), and ESTR +10–12bp in late 2027 as German supply continues to ramp up and QT remains in place. Our German supply and liquidity outlooks together suggest a similar story. German repo has nonetheless decoupled from the German supply/liquidity backdrop in a meaningful way since Q4 2024 (suggesting ongoing cheapening), which may indicate eurozone-wide supply and liquidity (Figure 2) is a better barometer for German repo conditions. If so, it would rather suggest potential for some stabilisation from here. records.text: Stress Testing and Potential Solvers for Diesel Shortages We next stress test OECD commercial diesel inventory levels in risk scenarios. Consistent with the analysis of European diesel (and jet fuel) markets led by our European equity analysts, we estimate that OECD commercial diesel stocks likely don’t reach a critical shortage inventory threshold neither in our base case (where Persian Gulf oil exports normalize by end-June) nor in our adverse scenario (where Gulf exports normalize by end-July). To understand potential solvers to prevent diesel shortages we next consider more extreme scenarios assuming the Strait were to remain effectively persistently shut. The starting point is the assumption that OECD commercial diesel stocks would continue to draw at their estimated average 0.8mb/d pace from the past 5 weeks barring any net changes in Gulf flows, crude supply, refinery output, diesel demand, and government policy.2 In a persistent closure scenario, whether OECD commercial diesel inventories reach critical shortage levels depends on the critical shortage threshold level, potential product export restrictions, and the extent of any additional of the following 3 solvers: Increases in the diesel share of refinery output. records.text: European Economic Perspectives11 May 2026 ab 4 Tracking stimulus − from budget outlays to production To recap, we track how the stimulus moves through the economy by looking at 59 indicators across different stages of transmission in a heatmap format. First, higher expenditures should become visible in the monthly budget data as the government starts disbursing funds. Second, we expect business confidence in the affected business sectors to pick up in anticipation of increased public demand. Third, orders and − with some lag − production data should pick up. Fourth, as capacity utilisation increases, firms may start to expand capacity, which should become visible in employment growth. We track the data for the two sectors that should be most affected: defence-related (including weapons, ammunition, explosives, and other transport equipment, which includes military vehicles) and construction (especially civil engineering). European rates are likely to stay directional with geopolitics in coming weeks, while other expressions may offer a better vol-adjusted performance. In particular, we continue to think 5y5y real rates longs present good risk-reward, given the embedded inflation protection and entry point. Moreover, this flow has likely contributed to the tightening of iotas in the sub-5y sector (breakevens outperforming CPI swaps). Intuitively, at some point, it may be justified to fade the flow pricing distortion, though of course this is always prone to the reverse of the "catch a falling knife" dynamic, and the geopolitical path inherently depends on what happens with the war in Iran. Directionally, this dynamic reduces our conviction to be long 5y TIPS, though we continue to recommend that position from a more fundamental perspective, whereas the tactical dynamic for the front end going into the strong carry period appears to have already largely play out. records.text: t the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, Brent’s fair value was closer to $90, reflecting tight post-COVID balances—OPEC supply restraint, strong reopening demand, and already depleted inventories. Markets feared that as much as 3 mbd of Russian supply could be removed, and Brent spiked to $128 in early March. In the event, only about 0.7 mbd of Druzhba pipeline flows were lost as the remaining barrels were rerouted, and oil finished the year in the mid-$80s. In 2026, the starting point was fundamentally different. We entered the year with swollen inventories and an estimated fair value closer to $60. Yet the shock itself was far larger—nearly 14 mbd of supply was effectively removed at the peak. Intuitively, this should have resulted in a much more severe price response. And yet, directionally, the framework was right. Brent averaged $99 in March and $102 in April. The model’s output highlights four key mechanisms shaping price formation in the current environment: 1. The starting point of the market matters. The price response to a given supply shock is not constant—it depends critically on whether the system begins in surplus or deficit, as captured by inventory levels. In 2022, with inventories already tight, we estimated the price impact of a 1 mbd disruption at roughly $15/bbl. In 2026, with inventories bloated, the sensitivity is materially lower—closer to $4/bbl. 2. Duration dominates the scale. The market is less concerned with the size of the disruption in isolation a

records.text: Demand for reserves pre-2015: Banks’ demand at ECB refinancing operations before 2015 would typically be driven by the amount of reserves requirement and net autonomous factors – aside from any profitable ‘carry trades’ potentially arising from non-standard monetary operations (e.g. 3y LTROs, TLTROs). In other words, banks were operating under a low-excess-liquidity regime (Figure 1). Post-2015: This changed with the introduction of the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) regulation, phased-in from 60% on 1 January 2015, to 100% by 1 January 2018. However, the simultaneous launch of ECB QE drove excess liquidity substantially higher, and in a manner that was beyond banks’ control. This supply-driven source of excess liquidity has made it tough to extrapolate banks’ demand for reserves arising from the LCR requirement. The new concept of excess reserves: As the ECB runs down its portfolios, absent any new structural operation, the amount of liquidity will at some point break below this new, theoretical amount of reserves which banks might want to hold onto – one driven not only by mandatory reserves and autonomous factors, but also by the LCR. Reserves will – at least initially – still appear in ‘excess’ but may no longer satisfy banks’ own internal requirements with regard to high-quality liquid assets (HQLA): we think this apparent ‘excess’ liquidity may thus be met with increased volatility in funding markets. In other words, even if the aggregate amount of reserves is adequate, bottlenecks could appear at the transaction level, creating the risk of instability in the short-term interest-rate market. records.text: The impact of the AI investment boom on China’s tech exports and growth is relatively modest, despite its enormous electronics manufacturing sector. The reason is that the core elements of the supply chain for leading edge semiconductor chips are largely outside China — though China has a dominant position in the production of many older-generation (‘legacy’) semiconductor chips. However, China does provide a vast number of smaller components that go to foreign producers, and we do see evidence that it is participating to some extent in the AI investment boom. For example, in China’s just-released April trade data, the three fastest-growing export destinations and import sources were all economies listed in Exhibit 11. Several caveats are in order before moving on to our conclusions: We emphasize the approximate nature of these estimates, given rapid technological n advances, shifts in some smaller parts of the supply chain, and lagging data on value-added, and the potential for currently available data (on GDP or prices, for example) to be revised in the future. Technically, the export and production impact captured here is somewhat broader n than purely AI investment related. More accurately, they measure the impact of exports of technology related to AI investment on each economy’s economic growth. records.text: Measuring the Wealth Effect of Rising Equity Prices in Japan As Share Prices Rise, the Proportion of Equities and Investment Trusts in Household Financial Assets Is on an Upward Trend Even amid heightened tensions in the Middle East, Japanese equity prices are reaching new all-time highs. A major factor appears to be the spillover from rising equity prices in the US, but another factor is NISA (Nippon Individual Savings Account). NISA is a program that offers individuals tax exemptions on dividends and capital gains, providing incentives for investing in equities and investment trusts up to an annual limit of 1.2 million yen and was launched in 2014 to promote a shift from savings to investment in Japan. The program has seen a steady increase in the number of accounts, but since the beginning of 2024, the number of new accounts has increased further, partly because the annual investment limit was raised to 3.6 million yen, and partly due to rising equity prices. Equity investment funds from retail (individual) investors through NISA have also been increasing (Exhibit 1). Under these circumstances, the ratio of equities and investment trusts in household financial assets is on an upward trend, and it is possible that the effect of rising equity prices in boosting consumption has been growing over time (Exhibit 2). records.text: ab 11 May 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives Germany: Fiscal stimulus tracker update and sector views Fiscal stimulus tracker and sector views updated through April German fiscal stimulus in defence and infrastructure is a key theme for our European outlook. We expect this to boost German GDP growth by c.60bp in each 2026 and 2027, and this growth contribution should be unaffected by the energy shock; in fact, our new GDP growth forecast of 0.6% for this year is essentially driven by fiscal stimulus only (we project 1.5% for 2027). We introduced a fiscal stimulus tracker at the start of the year (see here and Figure 1T r a n s m i s s i o n o f t h e f i s c a l s t i m u l u s for details), which gauges to what extent German fiscal spending is becoming visible in the macro data. In this note, we update our heatmap (Figure 2i s c a l s t i m u l u s h e a t m a p to Figure 4F i s c a l s t i m u l u s h e a t m a p − i n f r a s t r u c t u r e s p e n d i n g ) with data through April, summarise key developments and include bottom-up views from our sector analysts. Overall, the message is that government spending is rising sharply, with the macro impact very visible in defence orders, while progress in infrastructure spending is lagging and confidence in the sector fell in April. Our economist now expect hikes in May (off-cycle), June and August, to 5.25%. This could help PHP sentiment incrementally, from a relative rates differentials perspective. Adding the near-steady-state JGB holdings of roughly JPY154trn, the asset side of the BoJ’s balance sheet would stand at about JPY220trn if the JPY2trn-per-month JGB purchase continued. On the liability side, we have: Banknotes: just under JPY120trn Deposits of foreign central banks: just under JPY50trn Reverse repurchase agreements with the government: JPY10-30trn Provisions: about JPY10trn These items alone account for roughly JPY190-210trn. Unless these liabilities are sharply reduced, the BoJ’s reserves would be limited to at most JPY10-30trn. Such a contraction of reserves would place substantial strain on the short-term money market. Even though a steady-state is several years away, maintaining the current JGB purchase operations could cause reserve to fall below market demand before then. As happened in the United States in 2019, a sharp rise in the repo rate could occur. records.text: Second part of report title E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W Fortuitous timing: Near-term power prices have been relatively well shielded (compared to oil and gas markets) to the conflict in the Middle East due to a combination of seasonally weak demand and rising renewable generation. Indeed, renewable generation started the year strongly, supported by strong wind generation following a patchy 2025, with German wind generation up over 25% y/y year-to-date, averaging nearly 18GW. Average solar generation declined marginally y/y in April, but we expect solar generation to grow in the summer months to ease near-term power prices. An unexpected challenger returns: The sharp rise in gas prices since March has seen TTF prices move towards the top of the coal-switching channel, suggesting increased coal competitiveness in Europe. Coal generation as a percentage of fossil fuel generation has been well supported as a result, averaging 17% since the start of the Middle East conflict, up 1% on the same period last year. Although we see upside risks to coal burn from high gas prices, we expect coal generation this year to remain relatively flat y/y given coal-switching capacity is limited, particularly in north-western Europe, with German coal and lignite’s combined availability currently only around 14GW. records.text: 2 EU power and carbon update: On shaky ground Jason Ying, Commodity Desk Strategist | BNP Paribas London Branch Please refer to MAR disclosures and important information at the end of this report KEY MESSAGES We see upside to European power prices next winter on weather and gas supply risks, particularly in regions with high gas reliance and low switching capacity. Near-term power prices have been resilient to higher gas prices due to strong inflexible generation and seasonal declines in demand. France power prices remain the most shielded to the Middle East conflict. However, we expect this power price discount to the rest of Europe to narrow in the winter season. We see little change to EUA supply this year as policy intervention from the European Commission has been conservative so far. We expect few further changes with prices set to be range-bound near term. We maintain our view that balances will tighten later this year, pushing up prices and strengthening the correlation to TTF in the winter. Given volatility driven by the Middle East conflict, we update our forecasts to reflect near-term repricing, but still see year-end upside for power and emissions. records.text: os, absent any new structural operation, the amount of liquidity will break below this new, theoretical amount of reserves which banks might want to hold onto – one that is not just driven by mandatory reserves and autonomous factors, but also by the LCR. Reserves will – at least initially – still appear in ‘excess’ but may no longer satisfy banks’ own internal HQLA requirements: this apparent ‘excess’ liquidity may thus be met with increased market’s volatility in funding markets. In a demand-led system, we thus argue that the amount of ‘excess liquidity’ becomes floored with the portion of HQLA buffer banks want to hold as reserves. We estimate this floor at EUR1.3trn currently, rising to EUR1.4trn by the end of 2028 and EUR1.8trn by end-2036 (Fig. 2), based on a number of working assumptions (page overleaf). Plugging our LCR estimates, we find that ECB excess liquidity could reach this theoretical amount of LCR-driven demand by 2028, with demand at tender operations picking up from that year. NB: To project excess liquidity, we assume 3 approaches to net autonomous factors, which represent an important source of uncertainty. Considering the staged process presented by the ECB, the ECB could introduce new long-term operations by 2028, with its structural portfolio in 2030, although it could also adopt a more proactive approach by introducing these 1y early. COP: Banrep minutes retained a hawkish underlying tone, highlighting rising inflation, expectations still above target, resilient activity and a tight labor market. The board also flagged upside risks from the Middle East conflict via higher energy prices. Still, the decision to pause in April reflected a desire to avoid policy actions being interpreted through an electoral lens. Importantly, the tone suggests the hiking cycle might not be over, with room to resume tightening once electoral uncertainty subsides, as fundamentals continue to point to persistent price pressures. Risks to rates could intensify under a market-unfriendly electoral outcome, particularly as our models indicate that term premia in Coltes has room to decompress. On FX, we see upside risks to USDCOP , as we are now fully in the electoral trading window (the first round of the presidential election is on 31 May) and the MoF is buying dollars. The RBA raised rates by 25bp for a third n consecutive meeting this week and focused squarely on the upside risks to inflation, stating that “they do not attach equal weights” to both sides of the mandate, and that 4.35% “is not as restrictive as it was” in 2024. Hence, our economists still expect one further hike this year, most likely in June. As we noted in the past, this front-footed approach should help stabilize the forwards, and following the meeting, pricing now peaks at slightly more than one additional hike by year-end, with about 80% of a cut priced between end-26 and end-27. We think the policy stance can support asymmetry towards lower yields, especially if oil prices normalize earlier than in the RBA ’s assumptions or the inflation impact is smaller. Next week’s budget and potential cost-of-living measures could call into question how long monetary policy needs to remain restrictive. But past that hurdle, we see value in duration longs, as falling rate expectations tend to pull down term premia, too. records.text: Buffering: We seek to estimate here the potential demand arising from HQLA considerations, assuming the following: ▪ Banks’ average LCR set to drop to 130%. LCRs soared during the COVID- 19 pandemic as the ECB injected substantial liquidity, and we expect them to drop from high levels as liquidity declines – the average LCR across the eurozone has already fallen to 157% from a peak of 174%. We think 130% could be a soft target in a less ample liquidity regime. Indeed, by end-2014, a European Banking Authority report showed that banks’ aggregated LCR had reached 128%, right before the phasing-in of the new requirement began (Figure 1), and despite scarce liquidity at the time. LCRs then stabilised at around 125–130% just as liquidity started to pick-up. These inputs give us confidence that banks will want to maintain an LCR that is above the required 100%, closer to 130%. ▪ Reserves to account for 30% of banks’ liquidity buffers. The same EBA report showed central bank assets and exposures accounted for 30% of banks’ liquidity buffers, even at times of low excess liquidity between 2011– 2015 (Figure 2; excluding the 3y LTROs period). QE and TLTRO operations then boosted that amount. We believe that as central bank liquidity declines, banks may still want to maintain 30% as a floor (aggregated across countries). records.text: framework, dated 20 December 2024, it has moved away from a post-GFC, supply-led model centred on gilt purchases under the APF, and towards a system in which standing and repo facilities (STR, ILTR) provide reserves elastically as demand rises. As QT progresses and reserves decline, repo operations act as the marginal source of liquidity, helping to stabilise short- term rates around Bank Rate and flatten the effective supply curve. The ECB is further back in the process but has now clearly articulated a similar destination. Its March 2024 operational framework review signals a shift away from balance-sheet-size management towards a demand-driven system, where standard refinancing operations become the primary adjustment mechanism as excess liquidity falls. The aim is to decouple QT from interest rate control and avoid unintended tightening as reserves decline. How much is ‘enough’? The BoE has been relatively explicit on this point, publishing a preferred minimum range of reserves (PMRR), set at GBP375– 540bn and based on surveys of banks and liquidity needs (see BoE Executive Director Victoria Saporta’s speech from 7 November 2025). Crucially, this range is not treated as a target but as an uncertain, time-varying reference, reinforcing the case for a framework in which demand is revealed through repo usage rather than fixed ex ante. records.text: 11 May 2026 Quant Snaps Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG Figure 3: News-derived sentiment indicators Source : Bloomberg Finance LP, Deutsche Bank Looking Ahead Looking ahead, markets will focus on whether the recent improvement in risk sentiment can be sustained. The key macro events this week include U.S. inflation data, retail sales, industrial production, and jobless claims. Geopolitical developments remain important, particularly any response from Iran to the latest U.S. peace proposal and any update on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Markets will also monitor the upcoming meeting between the U.S. and Chinese presidents, as well as the Senate vote on Kevin Warsh’s nomination as Fed Chair. Conclusion In conclusion, last week showed that markets are no longer trading only on geopolitical headlines. Oil and rates remain sensitive to the inflation shock, but equities are increasingly taking their cue from resilient macro data, strong earnings, and improving risk sentiment. For quant strategies, this created a supportive environment for Pro-cyclical and Balanced portfolios, while Defensive strategies detracted as expected. As we move forward, the key question is whether earnings and macro resilience can continue to offset the risks from oil, inflation, and geopolitics. In a scenario where the Strait of Hormuz reopens, oil prices should move lower and inflation risks should ease, allowing Fed terminal-rate pricing to move lower, thus benefiting the trade. In a scenario where oil prices move higher, we like owning inflation protection. In this scenario, the trade benefits assuming the market does not price additional Fed hikes in response to the energy shock, which is in line with our economists' base case. Recent data also support this position. The University of Michigan consumer sentiment indicator has fallen to a record low, signaling weakness in consumer sentiment and reinforcing downside risks to growth. In addition, as noted in USTs Gazump Bond Bears After Payrolls; Reveals Positioning, the bond market appears to be positioned short. This short positioning makes the long TIPS trade attractive as it creates the potential for a short-covering rally if macro data deteriorate, while limiting the damage from strong data that the market already appears positioned for.

Morgan Commodities Research This is an important signal. The market is increasingly rationing demand not through the price of crude itself, but through the fuels consumers actually use. This raises a key question: can crude prices remain broadly stable around current levels—as our analysis suggests—while refined product prices continue to rise? Our framework and empirical evidence indicate that the answer is yes—and that this may ultimately become the dominant adjustment mechanism. If refinery runs remain constrained by insufficient crude availability, further rebalancing is more likely to occur through product demand destruction rather than through another major leg higher in crude prices. In that scenario, crude could stabilize in the low $100s even as product cracks continue to widen sharply. In that sense, the next phase of this shock may look less like a traditional crude spike and more like a refining and end-user fuel crisis. records.text: Diesel Margins Already Signal Scarcity Risk High diesel margins already signal scarcity risks even if estimated OECD commercial diesel inventory levels today (at 27 days of demand covered) remain somewhat above the inventories tipping point below which inventory draws historically produce disproportionately large upside price pressures. The minimum operational inventory threshold below which operational stress in the diesel market occurs is uncertain. After all, OECD economies haven’t faced significant diesel shortages in modern history. Exhibit 3 therefore looks at the relationship between OECD commercial diesel stocks as days of demand covered (horizontal axis) and average US diesel margins (the diesel price minus crude price) by stocks category (vertical axis) to conclude that the market has typically signaled diesel scarcity risk when diesel stocks as days of demand covered dropped into and especially below the mid-20s with disproportionately large upside pressures on margins. records.text: M Idea 6 The residual is simply the difference between the market forward and the PCA fair value. A positive residual means the forward is trading above fair value, or rich. A negative residual means the forward is trading below fair value, or cheap (Exhibit 6 ). We then convert the residual into a rolling z-score, so that the signal is scaled relative to the forward’s own recent history. We show PC1 against a representative forward such as 4y1y. When PC1 rises, the general inflation-forward curve level is usually moving higher; when PC1 falls, the curve is generally moving lower ( Exhibit 7 ). PC2 is the slope factor. It captures the main relative move between shorter-dated and longer-dated inflation forwards after removing the overall level move. We compare PC2 against long-versus-front inflation forward slope, such as 20y5y minus 2y1y (Exhibit 8 ). This gives us a statistical measure of whether the inflation-forward curve is unusually steep or flat versus its own history. PC3 is the curvature or butterfly factor of the inflation-forward curve. It shows when one part of the curve, such as the belly, moves differently from the front and long end. We compare PC3 with a butterfly-style expression like 1y1y+9y1y−2×4y1y to show that it is capturing curve curvature ( Exhibit 9 ). For the baseline rich/cheap analysis, we do not include PC3 in the fair-value reconstruction. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 To identify relative value, we need to separate broad curve moves from forward-specific richness or cheapness. We therefore shift from directional inflation pricing to a PCA-based mean-reversion framework for inflation forwards. Testing for mean reversion We expand on our framework previously published here. We calculate fair value of inflation forwards using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). It is a statistical procedure that allows us to summarize the information in a data set by transforming the input variables into different sets of fewer variables called principal components. The goal is to separate broad curve moves from idiosyncratic richness or cheapness in individual forwards. We compare each forward against a PCA-implied fair value that reflects the level and slope factors of the curve. The PCA is run on a clean set of underlying forward buckets rather than directly on overlapping market forwards. The key point is that each inflation forward represents inflation over a period of time, not a single point on the curve. For example, 1y1y covers inflation from year 1 to year 2, while 5y5y covers inflation from year 5 to year 10. Therefore, to build PCA input, we want forward buckets that comprise of the future inflation path without repeatedly counting the same period. We think the BoJ’s continued emphasis on n policy normalization over upside risks to inflation from fiscal risks and the present oil shock is unlikely to curb underperformance in JGBs. Evidence from G4 curves since the start of the oil shock suggests that a more front-footed hawkish central bank reaction can contain long-end risk premia via flatter forward curves. But in Japan, anticipation of a still-gradual BOJ approach has seen the market instead price a steeper trajectory out the forward curve. While a large portion of the increase in 10y JGB yields can be attributed to a normalization in curve shape to pre-GFC levels, the recent repricing has looked more out of step with fundamentals (Exhibit 5). Unlike last year, when the cheapness along the JGB curve was most pronounced at the very long end, underperformance versus the macro backdrop has migrated in towards the belly of the curve. And while idiosyncratic supply factors remain an episodic source of volatility, year-to-date trends suggest that macro dynamics have been the larger driver of higher yields and term premium. Without a more proactive approach from the BOJ, we think that higher yields can persist, with the belly of the curve likely to bear the brunt of additional cheapening pressure. As a result, we have raised our JGB forecasts to reflect a more durable risk premium across the curve, and now see 10y JGBs at 2.50% at end-2026 and 2.25% at end-2027. 9 May 2026 5 Goldman Sachs Gl

To maintain ECB reserves at this deemed satisfactory amount, demand at the ECB refinancing operations would need to pick up, to EUR180bn by end-2028 to offset the ongoing decline in liquidity coming from APP and PEPP QT. To satisfy this demand, the ECB could introduce its structural longer- term credit operations in 2028- 2029. We estimate that this shortfall in liquidity will then rise further, to EUR625bn in 2029, and EUR1trn in 2030, thus opening the door to the launch of the ECB’s new structural portfolio around 2029-2030. records.text: ECB vs Fed – different paths to a floor system: Both the ECB and the Federal Reserve operate floor systems, but the mechanism of reserve supply differs fundamentally. The Fed runs a supply-driven floor system in operational terms. This means that aggregate reserves are largely determined by the size of the securities portfolio, with QT and balance-sheet management acting as the main levers (see Front-end center: So close, yet SOFR, dated 13 January 2025). The Fed describes its long-run objective as a liability-driven balance sheet, but reserve supply remains asset-based, and scarcity risk is managed through QT calibration and backstop facilities. The ECB, by contrast, is moving towards a demand-driven floor system, where the marginal unit of liquidity is supplied through refinancing operations at fixed rates and against broad collateral. As legacy portfolio run off, reserve supply is intended to become increasingly elastic to banks’ demand rather than dictated by balance-sheet size. How much is ‘enough’? The Fed has gone furthest in attempting to quantify reserve adequacy. Empirical work from the New York Fed, updated in November last year, suggests that reserves become meaningfully scarce once they fall below 11–13% of bank assets, with money market rates increasingly sensitive below that range. records.text: About State Street PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of the prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. The interactive Country Inflation Series charts overlay against the relevant official measures of inflation, in all cases non-seasonally adjusted. records.text: iour over threshold. As set out by Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel’s speech, “Towards a new Eurosystem balance sheet”, dated 6 November 2025, the balance sheet normalization is deliberately staged (Fig. XX). The first phase is characterized by still-ample liquidity and redistribution via private markets, with refinancing take-up remaining limited. This is largely where the eurozone stands today. The turning point is not a numerical reserve label but behaviour: a persistent and broad-based increase in standard refinancing operations. This would signal that market redistribution is no longer sufficient and that banks are revealing stronger underlying reserve demand – a feature of a functioning framework, not a sign of stress. Only once short-term refinancing becomes structurally embedded does the ECB envisage structural LTROs to address longer-term liquidity needs. A structural securities portfolio sits at the very end of the sequence and would be introduced once legacy QE portfolios have run down sufficiently and structural liquidity needs are clearer. Even then, design principles imply stance neutrality, short duration and preservation of policy stance. The key message: normalization of the balance sheet does not mechanically determine liquidity conditions. The framework is built to adapt smoothly as reserve demand evolves. However, much will depend on whether the ECB supplies new structural reserves proactively or reactively, and on its willingness to keep up with a growing economy. The features and timing of new structural VLTROs will also be key, as will the new ECB portfolio and banks’ ultimate LCR-linked needs. ECB reserves above 9% of GDP linked to low vol regime: In the scenario outlined above, we think ECB reserves could fall below 9% of GDP from 2028 but remain around 8–8.5% for the following 10 years. ECB reserves amounted to 17% of GDP at end-2025; we expect this to decline to 10% by end-2027. Since the ECB’s fixed-rate full-allotment regime, there were only two episodes where reserves broke 9% of GDP (Figure 1). In 2012 it coincided with a sharp drop in market volatility, which picked up again only as reserves dropped back through 5%. That might seem low, but we note it coincided with the introduction of 3y LTROs, which sharply increased the duration of ECB liquidity, and with the absence of an LCR requirement. Then, in 2015, volatility again fell sharply as liquidity broke above 5% while banks’ LCRs were already close to 130%. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 10/05/2026 16:02:08 GMT Distributed on: 10/05/2026 16:02:08 GMT 10 May 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Global Metals & Mining Metals & Mining Industry Metals & Mining Date Periodical Iron ore curve steepening. Glencore Kazzinc developments. Results wrap Results season for the mining sector has wrapped, and we have updated our Metals & Mining Question Bank. Please message a member of the team for your copy. Iron ore: steepening cost curve from the Iran conflict Since the start of the Middle East ('ME') conflict, iron ore prices have increased ~ $12/t (spot is at ~$111/t), mainly driven by the upward pressure on the global cost curve and fears of diesel shortages. Vale estimates that industry cash costs (delivered to China basis) have risen by <$5/t to >$10/t since the start of the conflict due to higher diesel and freight costs, however, the impact by producer is "asymmetric" as costs for smaller producers more exposed to trucking and diesel have increased the most (by over ~$10/t). This suggests that the upper end of the cost curve has lifted from ~$95-100/t to ~$105-110/t. The majors are currently benefiting from a margin point of view (costs have gone up less than the marginal producer). Anglo and Vale are more exposed due to higher freight rates, however, Vale is mostly insulated through limited exposure to spot freight rates and fuel hedges, with reported unit costs (C1 + freight) up by $5/t (or ~$3/t after hedges). records.text: g (lhs) Regional banks' deposit minus lending (rhs) From this perspective, a central question is how far the BoJ’s reserves can be reduced. Prior research has suggested various upper-bounds for the necessary level of reserve, for example: JPY280trn (Sasaki et al., “Bank of Japan could halve current-account deposits to about JPY280trn,” 5 Nov 2024) JPY250trn as a long-term ceiling (Shiratsuka, “Toward a Guidepost for Quantitative Tightening: The Case of the Bank of Japan,” 9 Sep 2025) The latter study treats only reserves and banknotes as liabilities, fixing the long-term balance-sheet size at about JPY370trn. However, when we also consider the persistent JPY50trn of foreign-central-bank deposits and the JPY10-30trn of government reverse repos (Figure 3), the steady-state balance sheet could swell to roughly JPY450trn. The BoJ’s balance sheet today stands at JPY663trn. Our outlook is that, over the coming year, the combined effect of the loan-support programme expirations will bring the balance sheet down to just under JPY575trn by March 2027. After FY 2027, expirations of the loan-support fund are expected to decelerate, and if the monthly JGB purchase volume remains at JPY2.1trn, the balance sheet would fall by at most about JPY50trn. From FY 2028 onward, the annual reduction in the balance sheet is likely to slow to roughly JPY30-40trn per year. records.text: ins allow reservoir pressures to rebalance, which can support initial rates once wells are restarted. The more material risks are operational. Extended downtime can drive corrosion, scale buildup, or failures in artificial-lift systems such as ESPs. In mature, low-rate wells, restarting a damaged pump can become uneconomic if replacement costs exceed the remaining value of the well. But that does not mean the oil is permanently “lost” underground; in most cases, “lost capacity” reflects economics and restart costs rather than irreversible reservoir damage. Operators also have well-established mitigants— such as maintaining low flow rates instead of fully shutting in—which reduces the likelihood of these issues. Even if disruptions extend through late-September, we would expect aggregate long-term losses across the region to remain limited—likely no more than 800 kbd. And even that should be viewed as mostly recoverable over time rather than permanently destroyed capacity. Large-scale reservoir capacity is difficult to lose in the Gulf, where operators have decades of experience managing mature fields and temporary shut-ins. records.text: 2 Trump-Xi Summit Stays on Track Despite China’s Iran Concerns (2) - Bloomberg, 8 May 2026 Beyond Iran, the upcoming meeting between (14-15 May) Presidents Trump and Xi could afford further relief to EM FX, especially in Asia. Notably the USDCNY fixing was set at a fresh low last week, with China likely wanting stability ahead of the summit, as is usual before key meetings. Combined with post intervention JPY appreciation, this bodes well for Asian currencies in the near term. We note that Treasury Secretary Bessent is due to visit Japan this week too, which could add further impetus to JPY upside. KRW, in particular, would benefit from any further JPY strength as we have previously highlighted and maintain our short TWDKRW trade. Overall, we expect a conciliatory tone from the Trump/Xi summit and a message of stability rather than key breakthroughs. Trump may want to go into the meeting with Xi amid concrete signs that the conflict in the Middle East is ending or at least close to ending. Chinese officials have also stated they wanted the blockade to be lifted before the meeting.2 Even without concrete breakthroughs, however, we think the meeting will bode well for Chinese assets with positive repercussions for Chinese equities, CNH and China-related FX, both ahead of and following the meeting. 10 May 2026 3 Barclays | FX & EM Weekly Thoughts

LLC Shaun Zhou Shaun.Zhou@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-3348 Matthew Hornbach, CMT Matthew.Hornbach@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1863 Martin Tobias, CFA, CMT Martin.Tobias@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-6076 Aryaman Singh Aryaman@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1993 Eli Carter Eli.Carter@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4703 Rates market have calmed since April Since the ceasefire agreement was announced in early April, the US rates market has stabilized from the disorderly moves seen in March. Trading ranges and realized volatility have both declined toward pre-Iran conflict levels (Exhibit 1 ). Even as rates market calmed, developments in the Strait of Hormuz (SoH) remain an important driver. We use the Kalshi contract on SoH traffic normalizing as a market- implied proxy for the probability of a resolution to the Iran conflict. We estimate the UAE could return to 97% of pre-war levels by August. Iran and Iraq may normalize more gradually—potentially reaching 90% by August—while Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain could face longer timelines. Kuwait has indicated that full normalization may take three to four months. For Saudi Arabia and the UAE, risks appear more manageable given newer infrastructure, stronger reservoir management, greater operational flexibility, and less mature offshore systems. Qatar may take longer because production is tightly linked to gas-processing and condensate infrastructure, while Bahrain faces additional constraints from refining challenges after significant damage to the 380 kbd Sitra refinery. Is there a risk of long-term “scarring”? A key question is whether prolonged shut-ins could translate into permanent production losses. Our view is that these risks are likely overstated. Historical experience—including the COVID-era OPEC+ cuts, when producers collectively removed more than 10 mbd—suggests that most production ultimately returned without major, lasting damage to reservoir performance. In many cases, temporary shut-ins allow reservoir pressures to rebalance, which can support initial rates once wells are restarted. The more material risks are operational. Research Q1 2026 Global Earnings: Tech Drives Robust Growth In our takes on the Q1 earnings season in the US earlier this week, we observed that earnings growth accelerated to its highest in 4 years, and raised our S&P 500 EPS estimate for 2026 from $320 to $342 on the back of strong Q1 beats, strength in MCG & Tech, and higher oil & commodity prices (Q1 Earnings Takes: A Sharp Acceleration, Raising Estimates, May 04 2026). Globally, we see: Earnings beats solid in the US, typical elsewhere. The breadth of beats was above average in all four regions. The size of the aggregate beat, however, was strong in the US but only near average in Europe and Japan. In EM, the aggregate beat was well above average driven disproportionately by just 3 companies (Samsung, SK hynix and TSMC), excluding which EM missed modestly as is typical. Global earnings growth at a 4-year high. Global earnings growth accelerated from 15.3% yoy in Q4 to 22.6% in Q1, its highest in over 4 years. Earnings growth for the median company globally also rose sharply (to 13.3%). Earnings growth for Tech was strong in all regions on the back of AI-related demand, for Energy & Materials on higher oil and commodity prices, and for the Financials. records.Author: Akira Otani
records.text: In its “Sakura Report” (Regional Economic Report), which compiles and presents n micro-level information on economic trends, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) has consistently assessed over the past three years or so that private consumption has been supported by strong sales of high-priced goods accompanying the rise in share prices. Measuring the wealth effect of rising equity prices, we find that the effect has n increased significantly since the launch of NISA (a tax exempt scheme for small investments by individuals) in 2014, with a 10% rise in equity prices boosting consumption growth by about 0.3 pp. While this effect is extremely small for non-durable goods such as food and beverages, it is significant for semi-durable goods (which include many high-value items like clothing and bags), durable goods, and services (including travel, accommodation, dining out, and beauty services). Although there are concerns about downward pressure on private consumption n in the near term amid a significant deterioration in consumer confidence due to recent factors such as the conflicts in the Middle East, we believe that equity prices, which have risen to near all-time highs, will serve as a driver supporting the subsequent recovery and growth in consumption. records.chunk_id: US inflation: no shelter from 4% inflation?.pdf-1-0
records.text: Michael Metcalfe, Caroline Coughlin 11 May 2026 US inflation : no shelter from 4% inflation? At the beginning of March, Alberto Cavallo warned here that large energy shocks increasingly travel fast. The State Street PriceStats series for the US went on to rise 1.4% m/m (NSA) in March, the largest monthly rise in the US price level since our data series began in July 2008. This was mirrored almost exactly in the official data where the monthly rise excluding shelter also rose 1.4% m/m (NSA). As we detail in Figures 5–10 overleaf, there are signs that the immediate inflation rush from higher retail fuel prices is beginning to fade, but not enough to fully normalize April’s inflation readings. The monthly jump recorded by PriceStats in April was still the third largest on record. The only good news here is that this is largely baked into forecasts for the month (Figure 1). Nevertheless, this has pushed the annual inflation rate up even higher, climbing past 4% at the end of March and surpassing 4.5% on April 19, before only recently beginning to level off. Given the official headline inflation rate remains at 3.5%, it appears some catch up is overdue (Figure 2) and a headline annual rate above 4% looks increasingly likely over the summer. Real rates are headed into negative territory. As with the April data , the concentration of the inflation surge in energy prices means most of the attention will be on the non-energy CPI readings. Our sector breakdown remains encouraging. Food

records.text: TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA 12/05/2026 1 EM rates: Exiting 2y IBR–TIIE-F payer We exit the 2y IBR–TIIE-F payer trade that was opened on 6 May (see EM rates: Entering 2y IBR–TIIE-F spread payer), booking a loss of 38bp (USD191k). We are exiting the position as April inflation data in Colombia failed to act as a catalyst for higher rates. Furthermore, news on the Council of State striking down the pension funds transfer decree was sparking a leg down in the IBR curve. Even though the proximity of Colombia’s first-round presidential election on 31 May should drive further premium in the IBR curve, we prefer to exit now. To recap, we entered the position following the recent and surprising monetary policy pause in Colombia. The IBR curve should retain its premium, signaling either a higher terminal rate or stronger inflation ahead. With the presidential election less than three weeks away, the premium seems further warranted given the potential for ongoing political pressure on the central bank under a new administration. The day after: demand The demand side of this shock is not adjusting in the usual way. The initial impact of the war was a direct curtailment of activity in the Middle East—the epicenter of the conflict—driven by grounded flights and vessels and a decline in visitor flows. Next came the shortage effect. With the last cargo from Hormuz having arrived on April 20, Southeast Asia and Oceania were among the regions most affected by supply shortages. Price-driven demand destruction tends to emerge last, reflecting the relative inelasticity of modern oil consumption: transportation still needs gasoline and diesel, airlines still need jet fuel, and petrochemical plants still need feedstock. Fiscal measures can also dampen the effective price faced by consumers—for example through temporary fuel-tax reductions—thereby cushioning demand. Early adjustments are already visible: US driving and global flights are down 1% and 2% year-on-year, respectively (Figures 10 & 11). We expect these effects to broaden in May, as seasonal demand builds into the US summer driving season. records.text: personal consumption is one of the key points in determining whether the Japanese economy can continue its moderate growth without falling into a recession. In this report, we measure the wealth effect of rising equity prices. A 10% Rise in Equity Prices Boosts Consumption Growth by About 0.3 pp, With the Wealth Effect Particularly Large for High-Value Goods and Services Consumption We measure the wealth effect of rising equity prices using macro data on private consumption from GDP statistics, based on an error correction model framework where: (1) the long-term equilibrium level of consumption is determined by factors such as the balance of financial assets held, and (2) consumption in each period changes to correct for the deviation between the previous period’s consumption and the long-term equilibrium level. Under this framework, we assume that when equity prices rise, the long-term equilibrium level of consumption increases, widening the gap with the actual consumption level, which in turn causes consumption to increase to close that gap. Exhibit 4 shows the wealth effect (the effect of a 10% rise in equity prices on boosting private consumption) since 1998, when all the data used for the estimation became available, and since 2014, when NISA was launched. The results show that the average upward boost since 2014 is about 0.3 pp, a significant increase from the average effect of about 0.1 pp since 1998. records.text: 2 Natasha Kaneva AC (1-212) 834-3175 natasha.kaneva@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 11 May 2026 J P M O R G A N There was also a deeper reason for caution. Our pricing frameworks are effectively trained on the modern oil market—roughly the past 25-30 years of liquid futures trading. Within that dataset, there is no true analogue for a disruption of this magnitude. To find anything remotely comparable, one would have to look back to episodes such as the 1956 Suez Crisis or even earlier geopolitical supply shocks. But those events predate modern oil futures markets—Brent and WTI benchmarks only began trading in the 1980s. As a result, they offer limited guidance for how prices should behave in a real-time, financialized market structure. Put differently, applying standard models to the current environment risks extrapolating from a dataset that simply does not contain this kind of shock. A third issue emerged when we forced the model to generate an explicit price path: the results initially appeared counterintuitive. In early March, assuming that the Strait would reopen by early May, the model implied Brent would average around $100 across March, April and May. At first glance, this seemed implausibly low given the magnitude of the shock. This intuition was informed by 2022. At the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, Brent’s fair value was closer to $90, reflecting tight post-COVID balances—OPEC supply restraint, strong reopening demand, and already depleted inventories. records.text: D EEP D I V E DEEP DIVE KEY MESSAGES The ECB is moving to a demand-driven liquidity regime with deliberately no quantification of a reserve target nor a clear timeline on future structural operations. Our LCR-based estimates suggest EUR1.3tn of structural reserve demand today – rising over time. 2028 could mark a turning point where reserves reach this ‘optimal’ amount. Estimates from the BoE and the Fed suggest reserves of 7-12% and 9-11% of nominal GDP is optimal. Similarly, past experiences suggest to us that ECB reserves of 9-10% of nominal GDP could be a key threshold in a low-liquidity- duration regime and estimate. Overall, our analysis suggests new structural VLTROs could be introduced around 2028-2029 with the new ECB structural portfolio around 2029-2030. We do not expect much upward pressure in front end bases until Q4 2027. Risks around German repo remains to the cheapening side but we equally see a prolonged stabilization as possible. On the more hawkish side, Chicago Fed's Goolsbee, Minneapolis Fed's Kashkari, Dallas Fed's Logan, Cleveland Fed's Hammack, and Boston Fed's Collins underscored persistent and, in some cases, broad based inflation pressures. Goolsbee highlighted disappointi ng inflation progress beyond energy, arguing that rate cuts are “not the only thing on the table” and suggesting some flexibility around further tightening if needed. Kashkari went further, explicitly dissociating from easing bias in forward guidance and w arning that a prolonged Middle East conflict or extended Strait of Hormuz disruption could lift inflation expectations and plausibly warrant hikes, potentially even a series. Logan, Hammack and notably, Collins echoed this view, favoring neutral statement language and stressing that higher oil prices and sticky inflation raise the odds of holding rates for a long period, with hikes a tail risk if inflation deteriorates. St.Louis Fed's Musalem characterized policy as neutral or slightly accommodative in real terms and saw “very plausible” scenarios for holding rates for some time, with upside risks to inflation. As Chair Powell indicated in the April press conference, the debate around the forward guidance language was “much closer” than in March. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise the co sts associated with making pricing decisions. An identically large payout would be seen in both contracts on a +30bp parallel rise in yields, specifically into the low-coupon Feb-46 bonds. records.text: Investment to train and operate artificial intelligence models continues to grow n rapidly, with capex from the top 5 US hyperscalers (mostly in data centers/’compute’) currently expected to be $750bn for 2026 (+80% yoy) and global investment likely to be on the order of twice that amount. US (and global) data center investment has large spillovers to several Asian n economies. Roughly 60-70% of data center capex consists of AI servers, storage, and networking equipment almost entirely manufactured in Asia. International trade data do not allow for a clean delineation between AI- and n non-AI related tech investment. However, the increase in Asian exports of related electronic goods to the United States from 2022 (the year leading up to the release of ChatGPT) to early 2026 has been over $200bn annualized. We estimate tech-related exports contributed 5.9pp to real GDP growth in n Taiwan—which dominates high-end logic chip production and AI server manufacturing—last year, a record. We expect a boost of 4.5pp in 2026 (assuming still-rapid, but decelerating, AI investment growth). Comparable figures for South Korea—the dominant supplier of cutting-edge memory chips— are 0.8pp and 1.0pp. Other economies including Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam play smaller but meaningful roles in these segments and/or significant ones elsewhere in the supply chain e.g. assembly, testing, and packaging of chips. Potential side effects – higher growth volatility in tech exporters, softer services exports? More reliance on tech exports could make overall GDP growth more volatile in AI exporters, particularly Taiwan and Korea, as the AI capex cycle has been very pronounced but could also slow dramatically at some stage. The boom in AI related chip demand also could reduce the supply (and increase the price) of chips used in other sectors (e.g. consumer electronics), potentially cannibalizing other goods production to some extent. More capable AI might ultimately erode services exports from the region (e.g. call centers in the Philippines, IT outsourcing in India). Regional competition also might erode pricing power or share for the leading firms/economies over a longer period of time—in particular, China is making large investments in its domestic AI ecosystem. Our regional economics team intends to explore some of these issues – particularly the possibility of negative spillovers to service-sector exports – in future research. 11 May 2026 13 Goldman Sachs Asia Economics Analyst For the

Our sector breakdown remains encouraging. Food, household furnishings and equipment, as well as healthcare products, all showed below average monthly gains in inflation. The main areas of concern for core inflation come from apparel and electronics (Figure 3). However, when we pull all this together into our more granular forecasting framework, it produces the same central estimate of core CPI, 0.2%m/m (SA) as in April. This proved to be a prescient call last month, but our modelling process does not allow for the usual distortion in shelter inflation this month . The BLS rents survey is made up of six separate cohorts, which are surveyed every six months. But the cohort collected this April was not sampled in October due to the shutdown, it was simply assumed to be unchanged (Figure 4). So April’s collection will capture a twelve-month change in rents. records.text: liquidity preferences. The current 15bp corridor between the Main Refinancing Operations (MRO) rate and the Deposit Facility Rate (DFR) acts as a guardrail, ensuring rate control while allowing quantities to adjust. In short, the ECB wants to discover an equilibrium level of reserves, not define it. Behaviour over threshold: As set out by Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel in a speech last year (ECB, 6 November 2025) balance sheet normalisation is a deliberately incremental process (Figure 1). The first phase is characterised by still-ample liquidity and redistribution through the market, with limited demand at ECB refinancing operations. This is largely where the eurozone stands today. The turning point is not defined by a numerical reserve label, but by behaviour: i.e. a persistent and broad-based increase in standard refinancing operations. This would signal that market redistribution is no longer sufficient and that banks are revealing stronger underlying reserve demand – a feature of a functioning framework, not a sign of stress. Only once short-term refinancing becomes structurally embedded does the ECB envisage providing structural long-term refinancing operations (LTROs). A structural securities portfolio sits at the very end of the sequence and would be introduced once legacy QE portfolios have run down sufficiently and structural liquidity needs are clearer. Even then, design principles imply stance neutrality, short duration and preservation of policy stance.

records.text: 2028 could mark a turn: We estimate that ECB liquidity will remain abundant throughout 2026, and ample in 2027, with limited demand at ECB refinancing operations as reserves supplied through APP/PEPP exceed banks’ needs. The following year could mark a turn. We think excess liquidity will drop to EUR1.4trn over the course of 2028, a level that banks may see as a minimum satisfactory liquidity buffer to maintain for their central bank reserves. Our estimate assumes a liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) of 130% and ECB reserves making up 30% of banks’ high-quality liquid assets (HQLA), on aggregate, with wide differentiations between countries. Given the ongoing loss of liquidity from APP and PEPP QT, we think reinvigorated demand from banks as the EUR1.4trn level nears implies that ECB refinancing operations would make up a total shortfall of EUR180bn by end-2028. To meet this growing demand, the ECB could introduce its structural longer-term credit operations in 2028–2029. Our estimate of around 50k is consistent with the fact that the unemployment rate has fallen by only a few basis points on net this year, despite average payroll growth currently reported at 76k. 5. Two distortions related to the AI boom have worsened the near-term outlook for core PCE inflation. First, after adding new AI features to software packages such as MS Office, Microsoft and other firms now charge a higher price for the new bundle than for the prior standalone package. The official statistics don’t adjust for the expanded offering and thus incorrectly treat this as a pure price increase. Second, the combined weight of software and accessories—where prices have also surged on the back of costlier memory—is 30x higher in PCE than CPI, apparently because the underlying survey incorrectly captures not only consumer demand but also some demand from small businesses. Together, these distortions are likely to boost the year-on-year rate of core PCE inflation by 0.4pp later this year. Combined with an estimated 0.3pp pass-through from higher energy prices, this will delay the renewed core PCE disinflation we have been expecting. We estimate the impact of overall tech exports on economic growth across regional Asian economies in recent years using two distinct approaches: 1) industry-level data on contributions to real GDP growth, 2) an estimate of the domestic value-added embedded in tech exports. The first approach is most reliable for countries with granular industry GDP data—specifically, for the electronics/computer subsector—but most EM economies do not publish this level of detail. The latter approach has different challenges — export data are more frequent and timely, but estimates of the domestic share of value-added lag by years, and price indices for IT equipment can vary significantly. As a result, the two approaches typically lead to different estimates, although we have reconciled them to the extent possible. (In some cases, country-specific data allow an alternative approach as a cross-check.) Sector views: Construction/building materials (Julian Radlinger) Throughout Q1 results, construction companies largely confirmed commentary from Feb/March that project requests are starting to increase, with actual construction activity possibly starting in late 2026. The Middle East conflict has added a new dynamic though: building material prices (cement, concrete, asphalt, etc) are increasing by 5- 15% as companies pass through higher energy, fuel and raw material (especially bitumen) costs. In a typical road resurfacing (repair) project, asphalt represents ~2/3rds of total cost; for new projects (a new highway, say), it’s ~1/3rd. Therefore, total project costs are increasing ~MSD% on average, which is likely to eat into the infrastructure project budgets and could lead to lower volumes, at least for as long as prices remain elevated, and possibly risk project starts being delayed. To be sure - we haven’t seen this happening yet. From the point of view of the companies doing the price increases, this may not matter if the price vs volume trade-off is balanced, but for other companies, lower volumes could outweigh. Several soft survey datapoints like the civil engineering parts of the construction PMI or the IFO survey in April do show some pullbacks in sentiment (PMI down to 50 from 54), which could be reflective of these risks.
