The sharp drop in dated Brent serves to highlight downside risks to oil prices. Simple betas to oil in this case imply that almost all currencies would rally against the USD as oil drops, with the ZAR, KRW and THB the biggest beneficiaries. The 15% drop in Brent since its peak (close on 29 April) has already corresponded to a c.1% drop in the DXY, a much higher beta than for most of the period of rising oil prices (with the exception of the first couple of weeks of the conflict). records.text: April CPI Preview We expect a 0.31% increase in April core CPI (vs. +0.3% consensus), corresponding to a year-over-year rate of 2.67% (vs. +2.7% consensus). We expect a 0.58% increase in headline CPI (vs. +0.6% consensus), reflecting higher food (+0.3%) and sharply higher energy (+4.6%) prices, reflecting the increase retail gasoline prices since the start of the war in Iran. This corresponds to a year-over-year rate of 3.68% (vs. +3.7% consensus). Exhibit 1 provides a component-level summary of our forecast. We highlight four key component-level trends that we expect to see in this week’s report: 1. Shelter. We forecast a sharp one-time acceleration in the shelter categories—a 0.50% increase in the OER category and a 0.44% increase in the rent category—reflecting the unwind of the downward bias in the index level from missed data collection during the government shutdown. With a six-month rotating panel structure, the panel group that should have been sampled in October—but instead had zero price change imputed because the BLS was unable to collect prices during the shutdown—will be sampled in April. For that group, April 2026 will effectively measure two months’ worth of increases, as April 2026 prices will be compared to prices from April 2025 (technically a bit more than two months at the current rate, because shelter inflation has trended down over the last year). Even if Middle East producers offer higher freight rates to attract tankers back into the region, ships may need to (i) change destination mid-voyage, (ii) complete current voyages and discharge, and then (iii) ballast back to the Gulf—adding another 20–40 days before that capacity is effectively available. This matters because the tanker market was already tight before the war. The global VLCC and Suezmax fleets entered 2026 with elevated freight rates, high utilization, and limited spare compliant tonnage. Meanwhile, gradual OPEC production increases and the expansion of the shadow fleet—along with the rise in floating storage—had already strained availability in the mainstream market. The war pushed an already tight system into acute stress. Recovery is therefore likely to unfold in stages: first, the rapid release of the ~130 mb trapped inside the Gulf over the first two weeks; second, a much slower normalization of tanker circulation, port scheduling, vessel positioning, and regional export logistics; third, the normalization of pipelines and refineries; and finally, the recovery of upstream field production (Figure 7). Refineries, too, cannot snap back to full rates after a prolonged shutdown. Restarts and ramp-ups typically take weeks—and in some cases months. records.text: M Global Idea 2 The US gasoline balance shows why the clearing mechanism becomes more painful over time. If imports recover or Hormuz reopens, gasoline cracks can compress and the macro impulse fades. If constraints persist, inventories fall further, prices may need to rise enough to force substantial demand erosion, and the shock transmits more directly to consumers. In the first quarter of disruption, the oil supply shock is largely about higher prices. Brent, refined products, and physical crude markets reprice to reflect scarcity, and the immediate macro effect is a squeeze on real incomes. A second quarter of disruption with continued price escalation would start to diminish the “transitory” nature of the shock and begin to affect firm input costs and margins; savings would no longer be enough to bridge consumers; and central banks would have to pivot from delays to policy stance changes. Our economics note that modeled growth risks from the oil shock differentiated a price led shock from a volume led shock. In a price shock, the question is how much higher energy costs reduce demand. In a volume shock, the question is how much production can continue when a critical input is not fully available. That distinction is central. A demand-led slowdown can be disinflationary over time. The nature of the shock matters. This is not a conventional price-led adjustment. The scale and location of the disruption imply that a meaningful portion of demand is removed through availability constraints, not price. In other words, part of the rebalancing happens mechanically—consumption falls because molecules are simply not accessible—thereby dampening the required price response. 4. The adjustment is shifting down the barrel. Rather than being fully expressed in flat crude prices, a larger share of the dislocation is showing up in refined product cracks. Based on these rough outlooks, we can infer that the balance sheet will reach roughly JPY450trn around 2030–2031. At that point, we think the decline in reserves could trigger an ‘X-day’ – our term for the date on which short-term interest-rate markets face a shock. Of course, if purchases are reduced more aggressively, X-day would arrive earlier. If BoJ were to reduce liabilities outside banknotes and reserves (e.g. foreign central bank deposits, government reverse repo), then X-day would arrive later. Finally, there is growing uncertainty around demand for reserves in a world with positive rates. When negative rates were introduced, Japanese banks seemed to adopt the practice of keeping only a minimal amount of reserves and avoiding holding the negative-rate portion. Recently, however, loan growth has outpaced deposit growth, narrowing the loan–deposit gap (Figure 4). Over time, loan growth should fill this gap, reducing banks’ incentives to hold long-dated bonds and increasing incentives to hold shorter-dated JGBs or reserves. Currently, the BoJ holds a plentiful JPY469trn in reserves. The sharp repo-rate spike experienced in the US in 2019 was triggered by regulatory demands that forced banks to hold reserve deposits even when doing so was economically irrational. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Kalshi Contract on SoH Normalization The Kalshi contract (Bloomberg ticker: KALSI5KS Index) settles to “Yes” if the 7-day average transit count through the Strait of Hormuz exceeds 60. While this does not necessarily imply sustained normalization, it captures the aspect most relevant for financial markets: recovery in oil tanker flows. Importantly, the contract settles on a single qualifying event rather than persistent reopening. Temporary measures that allow stranded tankers to exit could therefore trigger settlement without implying a durable resolution. Directionally, we view it as a useful market-implied gauge of how conditions in the Strait of Hormuz are evolving. Market in a stable local equilibrium If we naively extrapolate the recent local relationship, the implied range for the 10y rate in response to developments in the Strait of Hormuz would be approximately 3.70% to 4.15%, or roughly 45bp in total. We believe this range is too narrow relative to the underlying uncertainty and therefore understates the true distribution of outcomes. In our view, the market is operating in a relatively stable local equilibrium due to several factors: • Oil inventory buffers have absorbed a meaningful share of the supply shock. Our energy strategists estimate that observable inventory draws offset 46% of the disruption during the first eight weeks of the conflict. Including less visible inventory channels, the effective offset may have reached 60-66%

However, with little change to fundamental balances for this year despite all the noise, we expect supply tightness to push prices higher towards the back end of the year, boosted by winter risks and Europe’s current weak gas storage situation. Correlation among seasonal patterns: The gas-carbon correlation has turned negative since the end of winter, while sensitivity to European risk assets has risen sharply. This is in line with patterns seen through 2025, which we think will repeat this year. We expect EUAs to track TTF prices in periods when gas-fired power generation sets the marginal price in the European power market, particularly during peak winter demand, and to decouple from TTF prices and follow broader macroeconomic trends through Q2/Q3, when power demand is lower and renewable energy sources have a greater share of the generation mix. Risk appetite falling: Net investment fund length in EUAs has reduced by over 72% since peaking in mid-January, falling from 126Mt to just below 35Mt long, according to ICE Endex Commitment of Traders reports. records.text: M Idea 4 • Inventory buffers are finite. The latest data suggest that inventories, especially refined products, have already fallen below multi-year historical ranges (Exhibit 3 ). At the same time, the pace of weekly draws is running at more than five times the historical average ( Exhibit 4 ). • The narrow trading range in rates underestimates the risk of a nonlinear shock. Our energy strategists frame the situation in the energy market as a race against time. In the base case, Strait of Hormuz flows begin to normalize in June and recover fully by November. In that scenario, inventory buffers and temporary trade adjustments by the US and China remain sufficient to avoid a severe supply shock, allowing Brent to decline toward $90 by year-end. However, if the disruption persists for longer, those buffers may begin to exhaust before meaningful reopening relief arrives. In that scenario, oil prices may need to rise toward $140- 150 on a sustained basis to induce demand destruction. • The impact of $150 oil price on US rates would likely become nonlinear, as sustained energy-driven inflation pressure and growth deterioration begin to interact simultaneously. Treasury lending in repo could dampen funding vol but lead to smaller Fed n balance sheet over time. At this week’s quarterly refunding, the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee (TBAC) discussed the possibility of Treasury lending excess cash into the repo market rather than maintaining the entire balance in the TGA. The concept has historical precedent—pre-GFC the Treasury kept the bulk of its (significantly smaller) cash balance in the banking system rather than at the Fed. The direct fiscal benefits would likely be minimal, but such an approach would have implications for the Fed’s balance sheet. Had the impact of TGA volatility on reserves been sterilized over the last six months, weekly reserve volatility would have been approximately 70% lower (Exhibit 2). The BoJ intends to cut the monthly JGB purchase amount to JPY2.1trn by the January-March 2027 quarter, and it is currently implementing quarterly purchase reductions in line with that schedule. The purchase amounts by maturity bucket are set so that the purchase-to-issuance ratio does not differ markedly across maturities, while remaining flexible to changing conditions. Morgan Commodities Research At first glance, this setup argues for a fast rebound: floating storage would clear, ballast vessels inside the Gulf would load, ballast vessels outside would reposition into ports, and the supply chain would begin to normalize. However, reopening Hormuz would not, by itself, restore the global oil system to normal. The bottleneck would simply shift—from a physical chokepoint in the Strait to tanker availability. The numbers underscore why. Since the start of the war, the number of loaded tankers actively circulating in the global market has fallen by roughly 400 vessels (Figure 5). Some were pulled into floating storage; others were delayed by rerouting and congestion; and some were absorbed into newly lengthened trade routes. Even after these cargoes are discharged in Asia or Europe, the ships still need to make the return voyage to the Gulf before exports can fully normalize. Switch Option ▪ The cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) bond of a futures contract can change due to changes in yields and yield spreads. ▪ In environments where yields are low, CTDs tend to be low-duration bonds. ▪ If yields rise, low-duration bonds become less cheap relative to higher duration bonds, increasing the possibility that longer maturity bonds become the new CTDs. ▪ A long basis holder (long CTD, short futures) profits during each CTD switch because it sells the former (now more expensive) CTD and buys the new (cheaper) CTD to maintain its basis position. ▪ The value of this option is reflected in the net basis (BNOC) of the futures contract which could widen (cheapen the futures price). For Taiwan and Korea, inbound data center investment numbers are far smaller than their exports of tech products. Implications for our forecasts The ongoing boom in AI-related capex has a number of implications for the Asian economies we cover: 1. A positive driver amid the backdrop of the global energy supply shock. Coming into the year, we anticipated further growth outperformance in key tech exporters, particularly Taiwan. The oil shock has complicated matters, but on net our forecasts are even higher than at the start of the year for Taiwan and Korea (and above consensus forecasts in both cases – see Exhibit 12). In these two economies, the upside surprises to export volumes and prices from AI-related goods over the past few months outweigh the relatively modest drag on growth from higher imported energy prices. Elsewhere in the region, the situation is reversed – the AI-related export tailwind is helpful but unlikely to fully offset energy headwinds. The disadvantages are the assumptions needed to arrive at real-value added: 1) assumptions about the current domestic component of value-added in exports—the most recent data are 2022 figures, and tech supply chains are rapidly shifting in ways that could affect cross-border value-added, and 2) the reliability (or lack thereof) of price indexes for rapidly changing technological goods. Furthermore, the price indexes are technically the price of output, not the domestic value-added portion of that output, so implicitly this approach assumes similar trends in the inflation of domestic and imported components of tech products. We forecast 2026 tech export contributions by constructing a regression of each economy’s tech exports on US hyperscaler capex, and then using consensus estimates of 2026 hyperscaler capex to project forward those exports. For price indexes, we assume the trends of the past year persist. Given the pace of change in this sector, these estimates need to be considered very approximate at best.8 8 One challenge here is that we have only 13 quarters of data to work with. However, we do find that the average “beta” of our export categories to hyperscaler capex across key economies is roughly consistent with 2/3 of that capex being equipment from Asia, and total global capex being perhaps twice hyperscaler capex. In 2028, reserves will break through 10% of nominal GDP; it is notable how in the past, the OIS/BOR basis has had the ability to widen a lot more when excess liquidity was below 10%, even though it occurred during stressed episodes (e.g. sovereign debt crisis), we note. From 2028, should the ECB fail to introduce new structural operations, we see a much greater risk of more pronounced widening as any shock would potentially affect the funding market more significantly, if the past is any guide. However, US diesel margins at $58 (7-day moving average) are already just above the $50 level typically associated with this inventories tipping point (Exhibit 3). This likely reflects the uncertain length of the disruption and the rapid speed of OECD commercial diesel stocks depletion. Using timely US weekly inventories data and the historical relationship between US and OECD commercial diesel stocks, our nowcast estimates OECD commercial diesel stocks have drawn at a rapid 0.8mb/d pace over the past 5 weeks (Exhibit 4).1 Our subsequent stress tests assume a critical threshold of 20 days of demand covered for OECD commercial diesel stocks. This assumption is broadly consistent with 1) the inflection point in margins in the low-to-mid 20s days, 2) the diesel market not experiencing major physical shortages when OECD commercial diesel inventories reached 24 days in September 2022 and 3) the IEA estimate of a 23-day critical threshold for OECD commercial jet stocks (also part of the mid-distillates product group). 1 Using the historical relationship, we nowcast the change in OECD commercial diesel stocks as 1.9 times the change in US commercial diesel stocks. records.text: d market policy rates Source: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas Given the conflict’s prolonged nature, any re-escalation of tensions might see markets begin considering downside risks to growth after the energy price shock. This means markets can still price in rate hikes, but then the associated demand destruction from energy costs and restrictive policy rates should intensify hedging of cuts soon after. Conversely, if a durable improvement in the outlook occurs, yields still should remain elevated but some of the premium embedded for a longer -lasting hiking cycle may be removed. This is most pronounced for Bank of England pricing , in our view. Monetary policy is already restrictive and as an energy importer, UK growth is sensitive to the conf lict. We expect two rate hikes this year, but then three cuts in 2027 as officials move to resume policy normalisation. The market is already pricing in those hikes, but appear s to be inadequately discounting the risk of cuts next year with just 15bp currently priced . We thus think Dec26-27 Sonia flatteners are attractive. In EM, a similar story holds for South Africa, where we forecast two rate hikes (in May and July) but think the market has more space to position for cuts in H2 2027. records.text: 10 May 2026 Metals & Mining Metals & Mining Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG from our coverage. It was a decent set of results, with the shares trading up by as much as +6% intra-day, before closing down amid rising ME tensions late Thursday that weighed on the market. A key highlight was the cash cost beat ($1.66/lb vs $1.95/lb), supported by robust by products and reduced costs at Caserones. Although there are upward pressures on costs (diesel, sulphuric acid, freight), cash cost guidance of $1.90-2.10/lb has been reiterated (assumes $4,000/oz Au). A number of datapoints are expected over the course of next week, including Chile and Peru copper production for March, and China inflation data (CPI/PPI) for April. Data & news flow Mining operations have reportedly resumed on 7 May at two blocks of the Simandou iron ore project after workers ended a strike that began on 28 April. According to a report, the UK Court of Appeal refused permission for BHP to appeal against a ruling by the English High Court that found it liable under Brazilian law for the 2015 Fundão dam failure (the dam for the Samarco iron ore operation in Brazil). China’s BF capacity utilisation rate for the week ending 30 April stood at 89.6%, slightly down 0.1 ppt WoW.
